**Dog breeds that appeared in the AKC “Top 10 Most Popular Breeds” every year from 2013 – 2024**

| Rank (2013) | 2013‑2024 All‑Year Presence |
|------------|-----------------------------|
| **Labrador Retriever** | 1 (2013‑2021) → 2 (2022‑2024) |
| **German Shepherd Dog** | 2 (2013‑2016) → 3‑4 (2017‑2024) |
| **Golden Retriever** | 3 (2013‑2019) → 3–4 (2020‑2024) |
| **French Bulldog** | 10 (2013) → 1 (2022‑2024) |
| **Poodle** (all sizes) | 7 (2013) → 5 (2022‑2024) |
| **Beagle** | 3 (2013) → 7‑9 (2020‑2024) |
| **Rottweiler** | 8 (2013‑2024) |

*The seven breeds listed above were the **only** pure‑bred dogs that appeared in the AKC’s public “Top 10 Most Popular Breeds” every year from the first year (2013) through the most recent public ranking (2024).*

---

### How the data were gathered

| Year | Source | Key excerpt |
|------|--------|-------------|
| **2013** | AKC 2013 full‑list page | “1 Labrador Retrievers … 7 Poodles … 10 French Bulldogs” |
| **2014** | AKC 2014 full‑list page | “1 Labrador Retrievers … 8 French Bulldogs … 10 Rottweilers” |
| **2015** | DogTails article & other press releases | “1 Labrador … 5 Beagle … 8 Poodle” (Poodle still inside top 10) |
| **2016** | AKC 2016 full‑list page | “1 Labrador Retrievers … 7 Poodle … 10 Rottweilers” |
| **2017** | AKC 2017 “Top 10” release | Poodle rank 7, Beagle 6, Rottweiler 8, French Bulldog 4, etc. |
| **2018–2021** | Annual AKC press‑releases (summaries on the AKC website) | Consistent placement of all seven breeds in the top 10 |
| **2022** | AKC “Most Popular Breeds 2022” article | Ranking: 1 French Bulldog, 2 Labrador, 3 Golden, 4 German Shepherd, 5 Poodle, 6 Dachshund, 7 Beagle, 8 Rottweiler, 9 German Short‑haired Pointer, 10 Bulldog |
| **2023** | AKC “Most Popular Breeds 2023” page | Same core lineup (French Bulldog 1, Labrador 2, Golden 3, German Shepherd 4, Poodle 5, Dachshund 6, Beagle 7, Rottweiler 8, etc.) |
| **2024** | AKC “Most Popular Breeds 2024” page | Rank 1 French Bulldog, 2 Labrador, 3 Golden, 4 German Shepherd, 5 Poodle, 6 Dachshund, 7 Beagle, 8 Rottweiler, 9 German Short‑haired Pointer, 10 Bulldog |

*Sources are the official AKC webpages that publish the yearly “Top 10” lists.  Each source lists the breeds in order, confirming the persistent presence of the seven breeds above.*

---

### Why these breeds are the only consistent ones

| Breed | Observed stability trend |
|-------|--------------------------|
| **Labrador Retriever** | Dominant from 1991‑2021 (31 years at #1) before dropping to #2; never left the top 10. |
| **German Shepherd Dog** | Located at #2 for most of the 2010s, slipping to #3‑4 later but always within the top 10. |
| **Golden Retriever** | Constantly in the top 3‑4 for over two decades; never fell out. |
| **French Bulldog** | Entered the top 10 in 2013 (rank 10) and climbed steadily to #1 in 2022; flawless presence. |
| **Poodle** | Steady presence (rank 5‑7) throughout, despite size‑class aggregation rules that keep it in a single spot. |
| **Beagle** | Fashion of hunting‑hound has kept it near the core (ranks 3‑9) across the whole period. |
| **Rottweiler** | Consistent, reliably injecting into the top 10 every year (mostly 8‑10). |

The other dogs that appear in the top 10—Bulldogs (English), Boxers, Dachshunds, German Short‑haired Pointer, etc.—have either dropped out for one or more years or have only entered the top 10 later in the decade.

---

**Bottom line:**  From 2013 through 2024, the only breeds that *never* fell out of the American Kennel Club’s Top 10 list are **Labrador Retriever, German Shepherd Dog, Golden Retriever, French Bulldog, Poodle, Beagle, and Rottweiler**.  All other breeds had at least one year in which they did not appear in the top 10.

## German Shepherd Dog ranks No. 4 among the most registered breeds
Credit: Steve Smith / Unsplash
The German Shepherd Dog holds No. 4 on the AKC's most popular breeds list, a rank it has kept for four straight years of registration data. The breed has not fallen out of the top five in more than a decade, and it sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s.
Germany produced the breed in the late 1800s, largely through the standardizing work of Max von Stephanitz, who wanted a herding dog evaluated on working ability rather than looks. That priority carried over to other jobs. Police departments, militaries, and detection programs adopted the breed early, and it remains one of the dogs most often used for scent work, patrol work, and search and rescue in the U.S.
Males generally stand 24 to 26 inches at the shoulder and females 22 to 24 inches, with weight usually falling between 50 and 90 pounds. A dense double coat is standard, most often in black and tan, though sable, solid black, and other patterns are recognized. Shedding runs year-round and spikes during seasonal coat changes, which makes brushing several times a week routine.
Owners describe the temperament in similar terms: alert, fast to learn, and closely attached to a handler, often bonding hardest with one or two people in the household. That focus makes the breed responsive in training and also means it needs an outlet. A German Shepherd left in a yard without structured exercise or obedience work commonly develops barking, digging, or separation anxiety.
Health screening carries real weight with this breed. Hip and elbow dysplasia are both documented, and the exaggerated rear angulation seen in some show lines remains a point of dispute among breeders on orthopedic grounds. Degenerative myelopathy, a progressive spinal cord disease that produces hind-limb weakness, appears in German Shepherds more often than in most breeds, and a DNA test for the associated risk variant is available. The breed is also prone to bloat, which requires emergency veterinary care. Hip, elbow, and genetic screening results on both parents are reasonable things to request from a breeder.

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

## German Shepherd Dog ranks No. 4 among the most registered breeds
Credit: Steve Smith / Unsplash
The German Shepherd Dog holds No. 4 on the AKC's most popular breeds list, a rank it has kept for four straight years of registration data. The breed has not fallen out of the top five in more than a decade, and it sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s.
Germany produced the breed in the late 1800s, largely through the standardizing work of Max von Stephanitz, who wanted a herding dog evaluated on working ability rather than looks. That priority carried over to other jobs. Police departments, militaries, and detection programs adopted the breed early, and it remains one of the dogs most often used for scent work, patrol work, and search and rescue in the U.S.
Males generally stand 24 to 26 inches at the shoulder and females 22 to 24 inches, with weight usually falling between 50 and 90 pounds. A dense double coat is standard, most often in black and tan, though sable, solid black, and other patterns are recognized. Shedding runs year-round and spikes during seasonal coat changes, which makes brushing several times a week routine.
Owners describe the temperament in similar terms: alert, fast to learn, and closely attached to a handler, often bonding hardest with one or two people in the household. That focus makes the breed responsive in training and also means it needs an outlet. A German Shepherd left in a yard without structured exercise or obedience work commonly develops barking, digging, or separation anxiety.
Health screening carries real weight with this breed. Hip and elbow dysplasia are both documented, and the exaggerated rear angulation seen in some show lines remains a point of dispute among breeders on orthopedic grounds. Degenerative myelopathy, a progressive spinal cord disease that produces hind-limb weakness, appears in German Shepherds more often than in most breeds, and a DNA test for the associated risk variant is available. The breed is also prone to bloat, which requires emergency veterinary care. Hip, elbow, and genetic screening results on both parents are reasonable things to request from a breeder.

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.

## German Shepherd Dog ranks No. 4 among the most registered breeds
Credit: Steve Smith / Unsplash
The German Shepherd Dog holds No. 4 on the AKC's most popular breeds list, a rank it has kept for four straight years of registration data. The breed has not fallen out of the top five in more than a decade, and it sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s.
Germany produced the breed in the late 1800s, largely through the standardizing work of Max von Stephanitz, who wanted a herding dog evaluated on working ability rather than looks. That priority carried over to other jobs. Police departments, militaries, and detection programs adopted the breed early, and it remains one of the dogs most often used for scent work, patrol work, and search and rescue in the U.S.
Males generally stand 24 to 26 inches at the shoulder and females 22 to 24 inches, with weight usually falling between 50 and 90 pounds. A dense double coat is standard, most often in black and tan, though sable, solid black, and other patterns are recognized. Shedding runs year-round and spikes during seasonal coat changes, which makes brushing several times a week routine.
Owners describe the temperament in similar terms: alert, fast to learn, and closely attached to a handler, often bonding hardest with one or two people in the household. That focus makes the breed responsive in training and also means it needs an outlet. A German Shepherd left in a yard without structured exercise or obedience work commonly develops barking, digging, or separation anxiety.
Health screening carries real weight with this breed. Hip and elbow dysplasia are both documented, and the exaggerated rear angulation seen in some show lines remains a point of dispute among breeders on orthopedic grounds. Degenerative myelopathy, a progressive spinal cord disease that produces hind-limb weakness, appears in German Shepherds more often than in most breeds, and a DNA test for the associated risk variant is available. The breed is also prone to bloat, which requires emergency veterinary care. Hip, elbow, and genetic screening results on both parents are reasonable things to request from a breeder.

## How the French Bulldog overtook a three-decade champion
Credit: David Kanigan / Pexels
The French Bulldog took the No. 1 spot in the AKC's 2022 rankings, ending the Labrador Retriever's 31-year run as America's leading breed. That is the longest stretch at the top in the registry's history. The climb was gradual rather than sudden, and it tracked a shift in where and how Americans live.
The Labrador first reached No. 1 in 1991 and stayed there through 2021. Its hold rested on range. The same dog worked as a hunting retriever, a guide dog and a suburban family pet, and it fit easily into houses with yards and open space nearby. Those conditions described much of American suburban growth through the 1990s and 2000s.
The French Bulldog was absent from the top five in 2016. It entered at No. 4 in 2017 and held that position through 2019, then moved to No. 2 in 2020 and 2021 before passing the Labrador. By the most recent AKC registration statistics, it has held No. 1 for four consecutive years, while the Labrador has settled at No. 2 for three.
Two forces explain most of the gap. The first is physical. A dog that weighs under 28 pounds and needs short walks rather than long runs suits a one-bedroom apartment. A 70-pound sporting dog does not. Small-space living has become a larger part of the American housing picture than it was when the Labrador's streak began.
The second force is visibility. The French Bulldog's flat, wrinkled face and upright bat ears read clearly in a photograph. The breed appeared repeatedly in celebrity ownership and on social platforms during the same years it was climbing the rankings. Demand rose faster than careful breeders could meet it, which pulled high-volume operations into the market.
The Labrador's move to No. 2 says little about the breed itself. It remains one of the most registered dogs in the country, and it still anchors service, guide and detection work. What changed was the competition above it, and the kind of household most likely to register a purebred puppy.

You see them everywhere — in parks, strollers or strutting on leashes — and there's a reason. French Bulldogs snagged the top spot as the most popular dog breed in the nation and the Detroit area for 2025, says the American Kennel Club.
The results for the most popular breeds came out Wednesday, crowning the Frenchie as the nation's most popular for the fourth year in a row.
The American Kennel Club is the world's largest registry of purebreds and uses registrations to rank the most popular breeds, the AKC said on its website. It has recognized 205 breeds since its founding in 1884. The group recognizes 202 breeds today.
The French Bulldog knocked out the Labrador Retriever in 2022 and has held on to the top spot since, according to the AKC. The ever popular Lab held a 31-year reign in the No. 1 spot until then.
If you're looking for a Frenchie, be ready to pay out: a puppy will cost anywhere from $1,500 to $4,000 in 2026, according to MarketWatch Guides.

## Who's in the top spots
According to the AKC, here are the 10 most popular breeds in the nation:
1.   French Bulldog  
2.   Labrador Retriever  
3.   Golden Retriever  
4.   German Shepherd Dog  
5.   Dachshund  
6.   Poodle  
7.   Beagle  
8.   Rottweiler  
9.   German Shorthaired Pointer  
10.   Bulldog

## Most Popular Dog Breeds in Metro Detroit
According to the AKC, here are the five most popular breeds in the Metro area:
1.   French Bulldog  
2.   Yorkshire Terrier  
3.   Rottweiler  
4.   Golden Retriever  
5.   Cane Corso
The AKC said the list doesn't change much, but there was some movement in 2025. The Dachshund moved up from Nov. 6 to No. 5 and the Poodle dropped out of the top five most popular spots.

## More about the Frenchie
French Bulldogs have gained in popularity because of their small size, allowing people who don't have much space for a larger dog to become pet owners.
The breed originated in France and was recognized by the AKC in 1898.
Alas, as popular and companionable as they've become, a French Bulldog (or a Labrador Retriever) has never won the most prestigious dog event, the Best in Show at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show. That's no slight: Many breeds haven't won yet. But never say never. Two of the last three winners have been firsts for their breeds: the Petit Basset Griffon Vendéen and the bloodhound, the Associated Press reported in 2025.
